This relatively modest size at parturition is typical of torporific elasmobranchs, where neonates are fully functional and capable of delivering incapacitating electrical discharges shortly after emergence. The species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate body dimensions, a pattern commonly observed among narcinid batoids. In the coastal waters of the eastern North Pacific, where this species is predominantly encountered, females attain a substantially larger adult body mass than males, with the maximum recorded wet weight for females reaching 60,400 grams [Wwi = 60,400 grams]. This considerable mass disparity reflects the energetic demands of producing large, yolk-rich offspring and the polygynous mating system that characterises this species. Males, by contrast, achieve a considerably smaller asymptotic mass, with the heaviest documented individuals weighing approximately 13,300 grams [Wwi = approximately 13,300 grams], a value that aligns closely with allometric predictions based on the length–weight relationship established for this species.

Sexual maturation in this species follows a protracted timeline that is strongly influenced by the cool, stable thermal regime of its benthic habitat. In waters maintained at a consistent temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], male Pacific electric rays attain reproductive maturity at a total length of approximately 64.5 cm [Lp = approximately 64.5 cm], a size threshold that typically corresponds with the onset of clasper calcification and the production of viable spermatozoa. Females, which grow to a larger ultimate size, reach puberty at a somewhat greater total length of approximately 73.3 cm [Lp = approximately 73.3 cm], at which point ovarian follicles begin to mature and the reproductive tract becomes fully functional. The timing of these developmental milestones is consistent with the generally slow life-history pace observed in deep-dwelling elasmobranchs, where low metabolic rates and food-limited environments favour delayed maturation and extended reproductive lifespans. The sex-specific divergence in pubertal length mirrors the broader dimorphism in adult body size and is likely driven by the fecundity advantages conferred upon larger females.

The species demonstrates a maximum reproductive output that is tightly coupled to maternal body size, with larger females producing substantially more offspring per breeding event. When expressing this as an annual frequency, field data indicate that females typically produce 1 litter each year [F_R_i = 1 litter each year], although biennial cycles have been reported in some populations. The combination of moderately large litters and relatively infrequent reproductive events places this species at the slow end of the fast–slow life-history continuum among elasmobranchs, with a reproductive strategy that prioritises the production of well-provisioned, large-bodied pups over frequent, small-litter breeding attempts. This pattern is consistent with the energetic constraints imposed by a low-temperature environment.

The ultimate total length attained by this species also shows marked sexual dimorphism, with females reaching a considerably larger maximum body size than males. The largest recorded female Pacific electric ray measured 137.3 cm [Li = 137.3 cm] in total length, a size that places this species among the larger members of the Torpedinidae family. Males, by contrast, achieve a more modest ultimate total length of approximately 92.1 cm [Li = approximately 92.1 cm], a difference that is evident across all life stages. This divergence is not merely a product of differential growth rates but reflects fundamentally different life-history strategies: females must accommodate the physical space required for developing litters and are under strong selective pressure to maximise body volume, while males face less stringent size-related fecundity constraints. The pronounced dimorphism has implications for population dynamics, as the reproductive output of the population is disproportionately dependent on the survival of the largest females, which contribute the most offspring per breeding event.

Longevity estimates for this species, derived from mark-recapture studies and vertebral band deposition analyses conducted in waters at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], indicate that the maximum lifespan is approximately 5,840 days [am = approximately 5,840 days], corresponding to roughly 16 years. This extended lifespan is consistent with the general pattern observed in slow-growing, late-maturing elasmobranchs that occupy stable, low-productivity environments. The combination of late sexual maturation, modest reproductive output, and substantial longevity confers a low maximum intrinsic rate of population increase, making the Pacific electric ray particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic pressures such as bycatch in demersal fisheries. Comparative data from related species within the order Torpediniformes suggest that such extended lifespans are typical of the group, with several congeners exhibiting similar longevity ranges. The accumulation of somatic and reproductive senescence over this long lifespan remains poorly studied in this species, though preliminary observations suggest that reproductive output may decline in the largest, oldest females.
